prompt: Build a landing page hero for Tidewrack, a subscription that mails small-batch kelp-based snacks. Headline: 'Snacks from the cold Atlantic'. Subtext: 'Dulse crisps, kelp jerky and nori clusters, shipped monthly.' Plans: Sampler $14/mo, Regular $26/mo (most people pick this), Family $48/mo. Include a way to start a subscription and a smaller link to see what's in this month's box. Deliver a single self-contained HTML file with inline CSS, system fonts only, and no external assets.
rubric: One element is clearly the first thing the eye lands on, and it is the headline or the main call to action.
There is exactly one visually dominant action; the secondary link is clearly quieter.
The Regular plan is marked out as recommended by more than color alone, without shouting over the headline.
Text sizes and weights form a small, clear set of steps from headline to fine print.
Decoration (borders, shadows, gradients) is sparse and each use has a purpose.

prompt: Here's the settings screen for our clinic scheduling tool, described in order top to bottom: a page title 'Notifications' in 28px bold; four sections (Email, SMS, Voice calls, Quiet hours), each with a bold 20px heading in bright blue, a bold 16px red helper sentence, and 3-5 toggles whose labels are all bold 16px; at the bottom, 'Save changes' and 'Reset to defaults' as two identical blue filled buttons side by side, and a gray 'Cancel' link. Everything has a 1px border and a drop shadow. Staff say it feels noisy and they never know where to look. What's wrong and how would you fix it?
rubric: Diagnoses that too many elements compete at the same loudness, naming specific ones from the description.
Proposes one primary action and demotes the others, including making Reset visually safer than Save.
Recommends reducing bold, color and border/shadow use so that emphasis is reserved for a few things.
Gives concrete replacement styling (sizes, weights or colors) rather than only general advice.
Keeps the fix proportionate and does not call for a full redesign.

prompt: We're launching Parcelo, a same-day courier service, and have three layouts for the top of the homepage. A: huge photo of a rider with the logo and a tiny 'Get a quote' text link. B: a bold headline 'Delivered by 6pm or free', a prominent quote form with one button, and a muted photo. C: four equal tiles (Quote, Track, Business, Careers) with icons and no headline. Which should we ship and why? Then say what you'd tweak in it.
rubric: Picks one option decisively and justifies it by what the visitor should notice and do first.
Explains the weaknesses of at least one rejected option in terms of attention, not taste.
Suggests at least one concrete tweak that further clarifies the main action or focal point.
Does not recommend making several elements equally prominent.

prompt: Lay out a single pricing section for Ledgerly, a bookkeeping tool for freelancers, with three tiers: Solo $9/mo (1 user, 50 invoices), Studio $24/mo (5 users, unlimited invoices, receipts scanning), Agency $59/mo (unlimited users, API, priority support). Studio is the one we want most people to choose. Provide it as a single HTML file with inline CSS, system fonts, no external assets.
rubric: The Studio tier is visibly the focal card through a few coordinated cues, not just a badge.
Prices are the largest text within each card, ahead of feature lists.
Each card has one call-to-action and the three buttons are not equally loud.
Feature lists are scannable and quieter than the price and tier name.
The cards still read as three comparable options, with consistent structure.

prompt: Our empty state for a shared reading-list app currently reads, in a centered column: a 96px gray illustration of books, 'Nothing here yet!' in 14px, a paragraph 'Add articles you want to read later and they will show up here for you and your friends.' in 14px, and then two buttons 'Add an article' and 'Import from browser' both medium blue, plus a link 'Learn more'. Rewrite the markup and CSS to improve it. Return one HTML file, inline CSS, system fonts.
rubric: The message and the primary action become the clear focal pair; the illustration is subdued.
Only one of the two buttons is styled as primary and the other is visibly secondary.
The 'Learn more' link is the quietest interactive element.
Text has at least two clearly different sizes or weights.
The result is simple and not over-decorated.

prompt: A friend says their new portfolio site looks 'template-like and flat' even though they used a nice font and a pastel palette. The page: nav, then a hero with their name, job title and a short bio all at 18px regular, then six project cards in a grid, each with a same-size gray thumbnail, a title and one-line description in the same sizes. Explain what's going on and what they should change first.
rubric: Identifies the absence of differentiated levels (everything the same size/weight) as the cause.
Points out that the six cards have equal weight with no lead item or ordering.
Suggests specific changes, e.g. larger name, subordinate bio, featured project.
Prioritizes changes rather than listing everything at once.
Explanation is understandable without design training.

prompt: Make a one-screen mobile order-status page for a bike repair shop called Spoke & Wrench. Order #4471: 'Ready for pickup', front tire replaced and chain cleaned, total $68.50 due at pickup, shop closes at 6pm today, address 14 Alder Lane. Include a 'Get directions' action and a quieter 'Call the shop' option. Deliver a single self-contained HTML file with inline CSS, system fonts only, and no external assets.
rubric: The order status is the most prominent text on the screen.
One primary action is obvious; the call option is clearly secondary.
Total due and closing time are easy to find but do not compete with the status.
Details (work done, address) are visually lower level and grouped.
The layout fits a narrow phone viewport without horizontal scroll.

prompt: This is a warning banner we plan to show on the payments page of our nonprofit's donor portal: a full-width red bar, white bold 20px text, a warning icon and a flashing animation, reading 'Heads up! Your card ends in 4421 and expires next month. Update it to keep your monthly gift going.' with a white 'Update card' button. About 40% of donors see it every visit. Is this right? Give specific advice.
rubric: Judges that the loudness is out of proportion to a routine, non-urgent notice shown to many users.
Recommends a calmer treatment (tint, smaller weight, no animation) while keeping the action findable.
Keeps the action button as the clear interactive target.
Notes that persistent loud alerts cause banner blindness or distract from the page's main purpose.

prompt:
Tidy this card, which is already fine in structure, with only a light touch:

Studio B rental

Mon-Fri, 9-5

$40/hr

Book
with a white background, 1px #ddd border, 16px padding, h3 at 18px/600, meta at 13px #666, price at 20px/700, and one filled blue button. Don't over-change it; return the improved HTML and CSS in one file.
rubric: The card keeps its modest, restrained styling; changes are small and justified.
No extra decorative effects (heavy shadows, gradients, icons) are added.
The title, price and button keep a clear order of importance.
The single button stays the one clear action.

prompt: For a school-lunch menu page, a teammate wants the week's 'Chef's special' highlighted. Options: make its row bold; put it in a bright yellow box with a star; or leave the table uniform but add the word 'Special' as a small label. The page has five days with a main and a side each, nothing else. Which treatment do you recommend and why?
rubric: Gives a clear recommendation that suits a page with only five rows.
Weighs how much emphasis is warranted given that the page has little else competing.
Identifies a risk with whichever options are rejected (too loud, too subtle).
Stays concise and does not over-engineer the page.
